examples.question_text:
Juice and water are mixed in the ratio $7:4$. There are $86$ mL of water. Find:
(a) the total drink
(b) how much more juice than water there is.
examples.solution_text:
Water represents $4$ parts.
$4\text{ parts}=86\text{ mL}$
$1\text{ part}=86\div4=21.5\text{ mL}$
(a) $7+4=11\text{ parts}$
$11\text{ parts}=11\times21.5=236.5\text{ mL}$
(b) $7-4=3\text{ parts}$
$3\text{ parts}=3\times21.5=64.5\text{ mL}$
There is $64.5$ mL more juice than water.

examples.question_text:
Nina, Omar and Priya share a prize in the ratio $6:9:4$. Omar receives $\$315$. Find:
(a) Nina's and Priya's shares
(b) the total prize
(c) how much more Omar receives than Priya.
examples.solution_text:
Omar represents $9$ parts.
$9\text{ parts}=\$315$
$1\text{ part}=315\div9=\$35$
(a) Nina: $6\times35=\$210$.
Priya: $4\times35=\$140$.
(b) $6+9+4=19\text{ parts}$
Total: $19\times35=\$665$.
(c) $9-4=5\text{ parts}$
Difference: $5\times35=\$175$.

examples.question_text: A recipe uses $21$ g of flour for every $14$ g of butter. Tessa uses $86$ g of butter. How much flour does she need?
examples.solution_text:
Simplify the flour-to-butter ratio.
$21:14=3:2$
Butter represents $2$ parts.
$2\text{ parts}=86\text{ g}$
$1\text{ part}=86\div2=43\text{ g}$
$3\text{ parts}=3\times43=129\text{ g}$
She needs $129$ g of flour.

examples.question_text: The ratio of novels to reference books is $7:4$. There are $32$ reference books. Some novels are borrowed and the ratio becomes $3:2$. The reference books stay on the shelf. How many novels were borrowed?
examples.solution_text:
At first, reference books represent $4$ parts.
$1\text{ part}=32\div4=8\text{ books}$
Novels at first: $7\times8=56$.
In the new ratio, the same $32$ books represent $2$ parts.
$1\text{ new part}=32\div2=16\text{ books}$
Novels now: $3\times16=48$.
$56-48=8$ novels were borrowed.

The question hides the width; the solution labels it correctly. The opening phantom gutter aligns the continuation equals sign without changing the calculation.
